questions.title: Flagged transactions
questions.stem:
A fraud model flags 2% of all card transactions for review. Fraud makes up 0.5% of transactions, and the model flags 90% of fraudulent transactions.

A transaction has been flagged. What is the probability that it is fraudulent? Round your answer to three decimal places (for example, 0.123).
questions.explain:
Use Bayes' theorem. The overall flag rate is given, so you don't need the law of total probability.

P(fraud∣flag)=P(flag∣fraud)P(fraud)P(flag)=0.90×0.0050.02=0.225

Check with counts: of 10,000 transactions, 50 are fraud and 45 of those are flagged. 200 are flagged in total. 45 / 200 = 0.225.
questions.ref: Cheatsheet page 2: Core rules, Bayes with counts

questions.title: Nightly jobs
questions.stem:
A data pipeline runs 8 independent jobs each night. Each job fails with probability 0.03.

What is the probability that at least one job fails tonight? Round your answer to three decimal places (for example, 0.123).
questions.explain:
"At least one" is the complement of "none".

P(none fail)=0.978=0.7837, so P(at least one)=1−0.7837=0.216.

questions.title: Audit sample
questions.stem:
A batch holds 25 records, and 5 of them are corrupted. An analyst picks 4 records at random, without replacement.

What is the probability that exactly one of the 4 records is corrupted? Round your answer to three decimal places (for example, 0.123).
questions.explain:
Sampling without replacement from a finite pool is hypergeometric. Choose 1 of the 5 corrupted records and 3 of the 20 clean ones.

(51)(203)(254)=5×114012650=0.451

A binomial with p = 0.2 gives 0.410, which is wrong here because the draws are not independent.
questions.ref: Cheatsheet page 2: Which distribution, Distribution facts

questions.title: Three suppliers
questions.stem:
A plant buys one part from three suppliers. Supplier A delivers 50% of the parts, B delivers 30%, and C delivers 20%. Their defect rates are 1%, 2%, and 4%.

A part picked at random is defective. What is the probability that it came from supplier C? Round your answer to three decimal places (for example, 0.123).
questions.explain:
First get the overall defect rate with the law of total probability: 0.5×0.01+0.3×0.02+0.2×0.04=0.019.

Then apply Bayes: P(C∣defect)=0.2×0.040.019=0.421.

C supplies a fifth of the parts but causes about two fifths of the defects.

questions.title: Retry budget
questions.stem:
A support bot resolves a ticket with probability 0.6 on each attempt, independently of earlier attempts. It stops as soon as the ticket is resolved, and it makes at most 3 attempts.

What is the expected number of attempts per ticket? Round your answer to three decimal places (for example, 0.123).
questions.explain:
Add up the probability that each attempt happens. Attempt 1 always happens. Attempt 2 happens if attempt 1 failed (0.4). Attempt 3 happens if the first two failed (0.16).

E=1+0.4+0.16=1.560

The same answer from the distribution: 1 attempt with probability 0.6, 2 with 0.24, and 3 with 0.16.

questions.title: Churn count
questions.stem:
Twelve customers each churn this month with probability 0.15, independently of each other.

What is the probability that exactly 2 of them churn? Round your answer to three decimal places (for example, 0.123).
questions.explain:
A fixed number of independent trials with the same probability is binomial.

(122)×0.152×0.8510=66×0.0225×0.1969=0.292

questions.title: Signups per hour
questions.stem:
A site gets 2.5 signups per hour on average, and the number of signups in an hour follows a Poisson distribution.

What is the probability of at least 3 signups in the next hour? Round your answer to three decimal places (for example, 0.123).
questions.explain:
Use the complement: P(X≥3)=1−P(0)−P(1)−P(2).

P(X≤2)=e−2.5(1+2.5+2.522)=0.0821×6.625=0.544, so the answer is 1−0.544=0.456.

questions.title: Delivery times
questions.stem:
Delivery times are normally distributed with a mean of 40 minutes and a standard deviation of 6 minutes.

About what share of deliveries take between 34 and 52 minutes?

options.text: About 0.68
options.why: That is the share within 1 standard deviation on both sides: 34 to 46 minutes.

options.text: About 0.815
options.why: 34 is 1 standard deviation below the mean and 52 is 2 above: 0.34 + 0.475.

options.text: About 0.84
options.why: That is the share below 1 standard deviation above the mean.

options.text: About 0.95
options.why: That is the share within 2 standard deviations on both sides: 28 to 52 minutes.

options.text: About 0.975
options.why: That is the share below 2 standard deviations above the mean.

questions.explain:
Convert both ends to z-scores: 34 is at z = -1 and 52 is at z = 2. From the 68-95-99.7 rule, half of 68% lies between -1 and 0, and half of 95% lies between 0 and 2.

0.34 + 0.475 = 0.815.

A calculator gives 0.819, because the rule rounds its percentages. 0.815 is still the closest option.

questions.title: Redraw
questions.stem:
A deck has 12 cards, and 3 of them are gold. You draw 4 cards. If none of them is gold, you set those 4 cards aside and draw 4 new cards from the remaining 8. Otherwise you keep your hand.

What is the probability that your final hand holds at least one gold card? Round your answer to three decimal places (for example, 0.123).
questions.explain:
You end with no gold card only if both draws miss. Track what is left in the deck at each stage.

First draw misses: (94)/(124)=126/495=0.2545.

The remaining 8 cards hold all 3 gold cards and 5 others. Second draw misses: (54)/(84)=5/70=0.0714.

1−0.2545×0.0714=0.982

questions.title: Converted visitors
questions.stem:
Of 200 visitors, 120 used the mobile app and 80 used the website. 45 of the mobile visitors bought something, and 25 of the website visitors did.

A visitor who bought something is picked at random. What is the probability that this visitor used the mobile app? Round your answer to three decimal places (for example, 0.123).
questions.explain:
Condition on the buyers. There are 45 + 25 = 70 buyers, and 45 of them used the app.

P(mobile∣bought)=45/70=0.643

The question asks for P(mobile | bought), not P(bought | mobile), which is 45 / 120 = 0.375.

questions.title: Interval for a mean
questions.stem:
A random sample of 400 orders has a mean value of 52.0 and a standard deviation of 8.0.

Using z = 1.96, what is the upper bound of the 95% confidence interval for the mean order value? Round your answer to three decimal places (for example, 0.123).
questions.explain:
The standard error of the mean is 8/400=0.4.

52+1.96×0.4=52.784

The interval is 51.216 to 52.784. It describes the mean, not individual orders.

questions.title: RMSE by hand
questions.stem:
A model predicts 10, 12, 15, and 20 for four houses. The actual values are 12, 11, 15, and 16.

What is the root mean squared error? Round your answer to three decimal places (for example, 0.123).
questions.explain:
The errors are 2, -1, 0, and -4. Their squares add up to 4+1+0+16=21.

MSE=21/4=5.25 and RMSE=5.25=2.291.

The MAE is 1.75. The single large miss pulls the RMSE well above it.

questions.title: Survey of active users
questions.stem:
A product team wants to know how satisfied all registered users are. It surveys the users who opened the app in the past week and reports 91% satisfaction.

Which problem best explains why this number is likely too high?

options.text: Selection bias: users who stopped opening the app are left out, and they are likely to be less satisfied.
options.why: The sample covers only the users who stayed, so it does not represent all registered users.

options.text: Regression to the mean: an extreme first measurement is followed by a less extreme one.
options.why: Nothing is measured twice here.

options.text: Simpson's paradox: a trend in every subgroup reverses when the groups are pooled.
options.why: No subgroups are compared.

options.text: Multicollinearity: two survey questions are highly correlated.
options.why: That affects regression coefficients, not who is in the sample.

options.text: The central limit theorem does not apply because the sample is too small.
options.why: Sample size affects precision. It does not fix a sample drawn from the wrong population.

questions.explain: The team sampled from active users but wants a number for all registered users. People who gave up on the app can't be in the sample, and they are the least satisfied group. This is selection bias, of the survivorship kind.

questions.title: Logistic prediction
questions.stem:
A logistic regression for churn has an intercept of -2.0 and a coefficient of 0.8 on the number of support tickets.

What probability of churn does it predict for a customer with 3 tickets? Round your answer to three decimal places (for example, 0.123).
questions.explain:
The linear part is z=−2.0+0.8×3=0.4.

p=11+e−0.4=11.6703=0.599

Each extra ticket multiplies the odds by e0.8=2.23. It does not add 0.8 to the probability.

questions.title: Two reviews
questions.stem:
1% of accounts on a platform are fraudulent. Model A flags 95% of fraudulent accounts and 10% of legitimate ones. Every account that A flags goes to model B, which flags 80% of fraudulent accounts and 5% of legitimate ones. Given the true status of an account, the two models err independently.

An account has been flagged by both models. What is the probability that it is fraudulent? Round your answer to three decimal places (for example, 0.123).
questions.explain:
Compute the probability of a double flag for each kind of account.

Fraudulent and flagged twice: 0.01×0.95×0.80=0.0076. Legitimate and flagged twice: 0.99×0.10×0.05=0.00495.

0.00760.0076+0.00495=0.606

One flag alone gives only 0.088. The second review lifts it to 0.606.

questions.title: Sales calls
questions.stem:
A sales rep makes 6 independent calls. Each call converts with probability 0.25.

What is the probability of at least 2 conversions? Round your answer to three decimal places (for example, 0.123).
questions.explain:
Subtract the two cases you don't want: zero conversions and exactly one.

P(0)=0.756=0.1780 and P(1)=6×0.25×0.755=0.3560.

1−0.1780−0.3560=0.466

questions.title: Third box
questions.stem:
A shelf holds 15 boxes, and 4 of them are mislabeled. An auditor checks boxes one at a time, at random and without replacement, and stops at the first mislabeled box.

What is the probability that she checks exactly 3 boxes? Round your answer to three decimal places (for example, 0.123).
questions.explain:
She checks exactly 3 boxes when the first two are fine and the third is mislabeled. The pool shrinks after each box.

1115×1014×413=4402730=0.161

questions.title: R squared by hand
questions.stem:
A regression predicts 4, 4, 8, and 8 for four observations. The actual values are 3, 5, 7, and 9.

What is R squared? Round your answer to three decimal places (for example, 0.123).
questions.explain:
The mean of the actual values is 6, so SST=9+1+1+9=20.

Every error is 1 or -1, so SSE=4.

R2=1−420=0.800

questions.title: A wide gap
questions.stem:
A gradient-boosted model scores an AUC of 0.99 on the training data and 0.71 on validation data from the same period.

Select every change that is likely to narrow the gap.

options.text: Lower the learning rate and stop adding trees when the validation score stops improving.
options.why: Early stopping halts training before the model memorizes noise.

options.text: Increase the maximum tree depth.
options.why: Deeper trees add capacity, which widens the gap.

options.text: Raise the minimum number of samples per leaf.
options.why: Larger leaves smooth the fit and reduce variance.

options.text: Train on more rows from the same distribution.
options.why: More data reduces variance.

options.text: Add a one-hot column for every customer ID.
options.why: ID columns let the model memorize rows, which worsens overfitting.

questions.explain: A large gap between training and validation scores is overfitting, which is high variance. The fixes reduce capacity, regularize, or add data. Anything that adds capacity makes it worse.

questions.title: L1 and L2
questions.stem: Select the true statements about L1 (lasso) and L2 (ridge) penalties in linear models.

options.text: L1 can set coefficients to exactly zero.
options.why: The corners of the L1 constraint make exact zeros common, which gives feature selection.

options.text: Ridge regression has a closed-form solution.
options.why: The L2 penalty keeps the problem quadratic.

options.text: With two highly correlated features, L2 tends to share the weight between them and L1 tends to keep one.
options.why: This is the standard contrast between the two penalties.

options.text: Increasing the penalty strength always lowers the validation error.
options.why: Too much regularization underfits, and the validation error rises again.

options.text: Neither penalty is affected by the scale of the features.
options.why: Both penalize coefficient size, and coefficient size depends on feature scale. Standardize first.

questions.explain: L1 gives sparse models. L2 shrinks every coefficient smoothly and handles correlated features more stably. Both need standardized features, and both have a best strength that you find on validation data.

questions.title: The C parameter
questions.stem: In scikit-learn's LogisticRegression, you change C from 1.0 to 0.01 and refit. What do you expect?

options.text: Stronger regularization: the coefficients shrink toward zero.
options.why: C is the inverse of the regularization strength.

options.text: Weaker regularization: the coefficients grow.
options.why: That happens when C increases.

options.text: A smaller learning rate, so training takes longer.
options.why: C has nothing to do with the optimizer's step size.

options.text: Higher weight on the minority class.
options.why: That is class_weight.

options.text: No change unless the penalty is L1.
options.why: C applies to the default L2 penalty too.

questions.explain: C is 1 divided by the regularization strength, so a smaller C means a stronger penalty. Ridge and Lasso use alpha, which works the other way round.

questions.title: Loss that climbs
questions.stem:
The training loss of a neural network oscillates and trends upward from the first epoch.

Select the reasonable first fixes.

options.text: Reduce the learning rate.
options.why: Steps that are too large overshoot the minimum, so the loss climbs.

options.text: Standardize the input features.
options.why: Features on very different scales make the loss surface steep in some directions, so a given step size diverges.

options.text: Clip the gradients.
options.why: Clipping caps the size of each step.

options.text: Increase the learning rate.
options.why: That makes the overshoot worse.

options.text: Add more hidden layers.
options.why: More capacity does not fix an unstable optimizer.

questions.explain: A training loss that rises means the optimizer is diverging, and the usual cause is a step size that is too large for the loss surface. Overfitting looks different: the training loss keeps falling while the validation loss rises.
questions.ref: Cheatsheet page 4: Diagnose the fit, Gradient descent

questions.title: Both errors high
questions.stem:
A ridge regression has a high error on the training set and a similar error on the validation set.

Select what is likely to help.

options.text: Add interaction or polynomial features.
options.why: The model is too simple for the pattern, so give it more to work with.

options.text: Collect more training rows.
options.why: More data lowers variance. This model's problem is bias.

options.text: Reduce the regularization strength.
options.why: A weaker penalty lets the model fit more closely.

options.text: Switch to a more flexible model, such as gradient-boosted trees.
options.why: A flexible model can capture non-linear effects.

options.text: Apply stronger L2 regularization.
options.why: That constrains the model further and increases bias.

questions.explain: High error on both sets, with a small gap, is underfitting. Add capacity or better features. More data and more regularization are cures for the opposite problem.

questions.title: Forest or boosting
questions.stem: Select the true statements that compare random forests with gradient boosting.

options.text: A random forest's trees can be trained in parallel, and boosting builds its trees one after another.
options.why: Each boosted tree depends on the errors of the ensemble so far.

options.text: Adding more trees to a random forest makes it overfit more.
options.why: Averaging more trees lowers variance. The gains flatten, and the fit does not get worse.

options.text: Boosting usually uses shallow trees, and random forests usually use deep trees.
options.why: Boosting combines weak learners. Bagging averages strong, high-variance ones.

options.text: Random forests mainly reduce variance, and boosting mainly reduces bias.
options.why: That follows from averaging versus sequential error correction.

options.text: Gradient boosting is less sensitive to noisy labels than a random forest.
options.why: Boosting keeps fitting the remaining errors, including noise, so it is more sensitive.

questions.explain: Bagging averages many deep, decorrelated trees to cut variance. Boosting adds shallow trees that each correct the current errors, which cuts bias and can overfit if you add too many.
questions.ref: Cheatsheet page 4: Random forest vs gradient boosting

questions.title: Decision tree facts
questions.stem: Select the true statements about a single decision tree.

options.text: Standardizing the features changes the tree's predictions.
options.why: Splits depend on the order of values, and scaling keeps the order.

options.text: A fully grown tree can reach near-zero training error and usually overfits.
options.why: It keeps splitting until the leaves are pure.

options.text: It can capture interactions between features without you adding them by hand.
options.why: A split on one feature inside a branch of another is an interaction.

options.text: A small change in the training data can produce a very different tree.
options.why: Trees are high-variance models, which is why ensembles help.

options.text: It extrapolates a linear trend beyond the range of the training data.
options.why: A tree predicts a constant in each leaf, so it is flat outside the training range.

questions.explain: Trees are scale-free, pick up non-linear effects and interactions, and are unstable. Control them with depth and leaf-size limits, or average many of them.

questions.title: Choosing k
questions.stem:
You tune k for a k-nearest neighbors classifier. With k = 1, training accuracy is 100% and validation accuracy is 78%. With k = 200, both are about 70%.

Which statement is correct?

options.text: k = 1 overfits and k = 200 underfits. The best k is likely in between, and cross-validation finds it.
options.why: Small k gives high variance, and large k gives high bias.

options.text: k = 1 underfits and k = 200 overfits.
options.why: It is the other way round: k = 1 memorizes the training set.

options.text: Increasing k always improves validation accuracy.
options.why: Past the best value, a larger k smooths away real structure.

options.text: k must equal the number of classes.
options.why: k is the number of neighbors that vote.

options.text: k stops mattering once the features are scaled.
options.why: Scaling fixes the distance. The bias-variance tradeoff in k remains.

questions.explain: With k = 1 each training point is its own nearest neighbor, so training accuracy is perfect and the boundary follows noise. A very large k approaches predicting the majority class.

questions.title: How ensembles work
questions.stem: Select the true statements about ensemble methods.

options.text: Bagging trains each model on a bootstrap sample of the rows.
options.why: Bagging is short for bootstrap aggregating.

options.text: In boosting, each new model focuses on the errors of the current ensemble.
options.why: It fits the residuals or reweights the misclassified rows.

options.text: Out-of-bag rows give a random forest a validation estimate without a separate holdout.
options.why: Each tree is scored on the rows its bootstrap sample left out.

options.text: A random forest considers every feature at every split.
options.why: It considers a random subset, which decorrelates the trees.

options.text: Stacking averages the base models with fixed, equal weights.
options.why: Stacking trains a meta-model on out-of-fold predictions. Equal weights is plain averaging.

questions.explain: Bagging and random feature subsets make trees differ so that averaging helps. Boosting is sequential. Stacking learns how to combine models.
questions.ref: Cheatsheet page 4: Random forest vs gradient boosting

questions.title: Naive Bayes
questions.stem: Select the true statements about a naive Bayes classifier.

options.text: It assumes the features are independent of each other given the class.
options.why: That is the naive assumption.

options.text: Strongly correlated features make its probabilities overconfident.
options.why: Correlated evidence is counted more than once.

options.text: A feature value never seen with a class gives a zero probability unless you apply smoothing.
options.why: One zero factor wipes out the product. Laplace smoothing fixes it.

options.text: It needs feature scaling because it is distance-based.
options.why: It multiplies per-feature likelihoods and uses no distances.

options.text: It can't be trained when there are more features than rows.
options.why: Each feature is estimated on its own, so it copes well with many features, as in text.

questions.explain: Naive Bayes applies Bayes' rule with a strong independence shortcut. It is fast and works with little data, but its probabilities are poorly calibrated when features overlap.

questions.title: Raising the threshold
questions.stem:
A churn classifier outputs probabilities. You raise the decision threshold from 0.5 to 0.8.

Select the statements that are guaranteed to hold.

options.text: The number of predicted positives does not increase.
options.why: Every row scored at 0.8 or more was already at 0.5 or more.

options.text: Recall does not increase.
options.why: True positives can only stay or drop, and the number of actual positives is fixed.

options.text: Precision increases.
options.why: It usually rises, but it is not guaranteed. It can fall if the rows you drop are mostly true positives.

options.text: ROC AUC stays the same.
options.why: AUC is computed over all thresholds, from the scores alone.

options.text: The false positive rate does not increase.
options.why: False positives can only stay or drop, and the number of actual negatives is fixed.

questions.explain: A higher threshold predicts fewer positives. Recall and the false positive rate can only fall or stay. Precision usually rises, which is why you raise the threshold to hit a precision bar, but only "usually".

questions.title: Reading ROC AUC
questions.stem: Select the true statements about ROC AUC.

options.text: It is the probability that a randomly chosen positive gets a higher score than a randomly chosen negative.
options.why: This is the ranking interpretation.

options.text: It does not change if you apply a strictly increasing transformation to the scores.
options.why: Only the order of the scores matters.

options.text: A model with an AUC of 0.5 ranks no better than chance.
options.why: 0.5 is the diagonal of the ROC plot.

options.text: It tells you which decision threshold to use.
options.why: It summarizes all thresholds. You still choose one from costs or a target metric.

options.text: With 1% positives, a high ROC AUC guarantees high precision.
options.why: With heavy imbalance, a small false positive rate still yields many false positives. Check the precision-recall curve.

questions.explain: AUC measures ranking quality and ignores calibration and thresholds. Under heavy imbalance it can look strong while precision is poor.

questions.title: MSE and MAE
questions.stem: Select the true statements about mean squared error and mean absolute error.

options.text: The constant prediction that minimizes MSE is the mean, and for MAE it is the median.
options.why: This is why MAE is robust to outliers.

options.text: MSE is more sensitive to outliers than MAE.
options.why: Squaring makes large errors dominate.

options.text: On the same errors, RMSE is never smaller than MAE.
options.why: They are equal only when every absolute error is the same size.

options.text: MAE is differentiable everywhere, which is why gradient methods prefer it.
options.why: MAE has a kink at zero. MSE is the smooth one.

options.text: MSE and MAE always rank two models in the same order.
options.why: A model with a few large misses can win on MAE and lose on MSE.

questions.explain: Choose the metric that matches the cost of errors. If large misses are far worse than small ones, use squared error. If you want robustness to a few extreme values, use absolute error.

questions.title: Two percent fraud
questions.stem: 2% of transactions are fraud. Select the sound practices.

options.text: Report precision and recall, or PR AUC, instead of accuracy alone.
options.why: Accuracy is dominated by the majority class.

options.text: Oversample the minority class, then split into train and test.
options.why: Copies of the same row land on both sides of the split, which leaks.

options.text: Use a stratified split so that both sets keep the 2% rate.
options.why: Otherwise a small test set can hold very few positives.

options.text: Apply class weights or resampling to the training folds only.
options.why: Validation and test data must keep the real class balance.

options.text: Treat a model with 98% accuracy as clearly useful.
options.why: Predicting "not fraud" for everything scores 98%.

questions.explain: With rare positives, split first and keep the evaluation data untouched. Judge the model on metrics that focus on the positive class.

questions.title: Cross-validation
questions.stem: Select the true statements about cross-validation.

options.text: In k-fold cross-validation, every row is used for validation exactly once.
options.why: The folds partition the data.

options.text: Leave-one-out cross-validation trains one model per row.
options.why: It is k-fold with k equal to the number of rows.

options.text: With time-ordered data, shuffled k-fold can leak future information into training.
options.why: Use splits that train on the past and validate on the future.

options.text: Tune hyperparameters on the test set to get an unbiased final score.
options.why: Tuning on the test set makes its score optimistic. Tune with cross-validation on the training data.

options.text: Stratified k-fold keeps all of one customer's rows in the same fold.
options.why: That is group k-fold. Stratified k-fold keeps the class proportions.

questions.explain: Cross-validation reuses the training data to estimate performance. The split must mirror how the model is used: grouped for repeated entities, ordered for time series, stratified for imbalanced classes.

questions.title: Find the leaks
questions.stem: Which of these leak information that the model would not have at prediction time? Select all that apply.

options.text: Fitting a StandardScaler on the full dataset, then splitting into train and test.
options.why: The scaler has seen the test rows.

options.text: Using "refund issued" as a feature to predict whether an order is returned.
options.why: The refund happens after the return, so it encodes the target.

options.text: Computing target-encoding means on the training folds and applying them to the validation fold.
options.why: That is the correct, out-of-fold way to do it.

options.text: Splitting rows at random when the same customer appears many times and the goal is to predict for new customers.
options.why: The model sees the same customers in train and test. Split by customer.

options.text: Fitting an imputer inside a Pipeline that you pass to cross_val_score.
options.why: The pipeline refits the imputer on each training fold, so nothing leaks.

questions.explain: Leakage has three common forms: preprocessing fitted on all rows, features that come from the future or from the target, and splits that put the same entity on both sides.

questions.title: Who needs scaling
questions.stem: For which of these models does standardizing the features change the predictions? Select all that apply.

options.text: k-nearest neighbors
options.why: Distances are dominated by features with large scales.

options.text: Random forest
options.why: Tree splits depend only on the order of values.

options.text: Logistic regression with an L2 penalty
options.why: The penalty depends on coefficient size, which depends on feature scale.

options.text: Support vector machine with an RBF kernel
options.why: The kernel is built on distances.

options.text: Ordinary least squares with no penalty
options.why: The coefficients rescale to compensate, so the fitted values are identical.

questions.explain: Scaling matters whenever the model uses distances or penalizes coefficients. Trees ignore it, and an unpenalized linear model absorbs it into the coefficients.

questions.title: Encoding categories
questions.stem: Select the true statements about encoding categorical features.

options.text: One-hot encoding an unordered category avoids implying an order.
options.why: Each level gets its own column.

options.text: Ordinal encoding suits categories with a natural order, such as low, medium, high.
options.why: The integers carry the order.

options.text: One-hot encoding a column with 50,000 distinct values creates a very wide, sparse matrix.
options.why: Consider target encoding or grouping rare levels instead.

options.text: Encoding city names as the integers 0 to N is harmless for a linear model.
options.why: The model would treat the codes as quantities, so city 40 counts as twice city 20.

options.text: With handle_unknown='ignore', OneHotEncoder raises an error on a category it did not see in training.
options.why: It outputs zeros in every column of that feature.

questions.explain: Match the encoding to the meaning: one-hot for names, ordinal for ranks. Plan for levels that appear only at prediction time.

questions.title: Neural network basics
questions.stem: Select the true statements about feed-forward neural networks.

options.text: Without non-linear activations, a deep network is equivalent to a single linear layer.
options.why: A composition of linear maps is linear.

options.text: ReLU reduces the vanishing-gradient problem compared with the sigmoid.
options.why: Its gradient is 1 for positive inputs, and it does not saturate there.

options.text: Dropout is applied during training and switched off at prediction time.
options.why: At prediction time the full network is used.

options.text: Starting with every weight at zero helps the network train faster.
options.why: All units in a layer would compute the same thing and receive the same update.

options.text: The outputs of a softmax layer add up to 1.
options.why: Softmax turns scores into a probability distribution over classes.

questions.explain: Depth is only useful with non-linear activations. ReLU, sensible initialization, and normalization keep gradients healthy, and dropout regularizes during training.

questions.title: Output layer for two classes
questions.stem: You build a network for binary classification. Which output activation and loss are the standard pair?

options.text: A sigmoid output with binary cross-entropy loss.
options.why: The sigmoid gives a probability, and cross-entropy is its matching likelihood loss.

options.text: A softmax output over the two classes with mean squared error.
options.why: Softmax pairs with cross-entropy, not squared error.

options.text: A ReLU output with cross-entropy loss.
options.why: ReLU is unbounded above and can output exactly 0, so it is not a probability.

options.text: A linear output with hinge loss.
options.why: That is the support vector machine setup, not the standard probabilistic classifier.

options.text: A tanh output with mean absolute error.
options.why: tanh ranges from -1 to 1, which is not a probability.

questions.explain: Regression uses a linear output with squared error. Binary classification uses a sigmoid with binary cross-entropy. Multi-class uses softmax with cross-entropy.

questions.title: Forest that memorizes
questions.stem:
A random forest reaches 99% accuracy on the training set and 80% on the validation set.

Select every change that is likely to narrow the gap.

options.text: Limit the maximum depth of the trees.
options.why: Shallower trees can't isolate single rows.

options.text: Raise the minimum number of samples per leaf.
options.why: Larger leaves average over more rows.

options.text: Train on all rows and stop using a validation set.
options.why: That hides the gap. It does not close it.

options.text: Consider fewer features at each split.
options.why: Trees become less correlated, so averaging removes more variance.

options.text: Stop standardizing the features.
options.why: Scaling has no effect on trees.

questions.explain: The forest's trees are too flexible. Constrain each tree, or decorrelate the trees so that averaging does more.

questions.title: Many irrelevant features
questions.stem: You have 5,000 features, most of them irrelevant, and you want a sparse linear model that is easy to explain. Which penalty fits best?

options.text: L1 (lasso)
options.why: It sets many coefficients to exactly zero.

options.text: L2 (ridge)
options.why: It shrinks coefficients and keeps all of them non-zero.

options.text: No penalty
options.why: With many irrelevant features, an unpenalized model overfits.

options.text: Dropout
options.why: Dropout is a neural network regularizer.

options.text: Early stopping
options.why: It limits training time and does not select features.

questions.explain: L1 does feature selection as part of the fit. Elastic net is a common choice when correlated features make pure L1 unstable.

questions.title: Confusion matrix
questions.stem:
On 1,000 cases a classifier has 30 true positives, 10 false positives, 20 false negatives, and 940 true negatives.

Select the correct values.

options.text: Precision is 0.75.
Recall is 0.60.
Accuracy is 0.97.

options.why: 2 × 0.75 × 0.60 / 1.35 = 0.667. F1 is the harmonic mean, not the arithmetic mean.

options.text: The false positive rate is 0.25.

questions.explain: Precision divides by predicted positives. Recall divides by actual positives. The false positive rate divides by actual negatives.

questions.title: Boosting settings
questions.stem: Select the true statements about gradient boosting.

options.text: A smaller learning rate usually needs more trees to reach the same training loss.
options.why: Each tree contributes less.

options.text: Early stopping uses a validation set to choose the number of trees.
options.why: You stop when the validation score stops improving.

options.text: Training each tree on a random subsample of rows can reduce overfitting.
options.why: This is stochastic gradient boosting.

options.text: Deeper trees always generalize better.
options.why: Deeper trees fit more complex interactions and overfit more easily.

options.text: Boosting can't overfit because each tree is a weak learner.
options.why: Enough weak learners fit the noise.

questions.explain: Learning rate, number of trees, and tree depth trade off against each other. The usual recipe is a small learning rate, shallow trees, and early stopping.

questions.title: Monthly snapshots
questions.stem:
Your data has one row per customer per month. You predict next month's churn and evaluate with a random 80/20 split of the rows.

Select the real problems with this setup.

options.text: The same customer appears in both train and test.
options.why: The model can recognize customers instead of learning patterns that carry over to new ones.

options.text: Rows from later months can be in train while earlier months are in test.
options.why: The model learns from the future.

options.text: The test score is likely too optimistic.
options.why: Both leaks inflate it.

options.text: A random split is invalid for every classification task.
options.why: It is fine when rows are independent and not time-ordered.

options.text: Stratifying the split by the target fixes these problems.
options.why: Stratifying balances classes. It does not separate customers or time.

questions.explain: Split the way the model is used: train on earlier months and test on later ones, and keep each customer on one side when you predict for new customers.

questions.title: Hidden-layer activation
questions.stem: Which activation is the usual default for the hidden layers of a feed-forward network, and why?

options.text: ReLU, because it is cheap to compute and does not saturate for positive inputs.
options.why: Gradients pass through unchanged where the unit is active.

options.text: Sigmoid, because its outputs are probabilities.
options.why: Sigmoids saturate, and gradients vanish in deep stacks.

options.text: Softmax, because it normalizes each layer.
options.why: Softmax belongs on a multi-class output layer.

options.text: A linear activation, because it keeps gradients constant.
options.why: Linear layers collapse into one linear map.

options.text: A step function, because it gives clear decisions.
options.why: Its gradient is zero almost everywhere, so backpropagation can't train it.

questions.explain: ReLU and its variants are the default for hidden layers. Sigmoid and softmax are for output layers.

questions.title: More ridge
questions.stem: You increase alpha in a Ridge regression from 0.1 to 100 and refit on the same data. Select what you expect.

options.text: The coefficients shrink toward zero.
options.why: A larger alpha is a stronger L2 penalty.

options.text: The training error stays the same or rises.
options.why: A tighter constraint can't fit the training data better.

options.text: The model's variance decreases.
options.why: Predictions depend less on the particular sample.

options.text: Some coefficients become exactly zero.
options.why: That is the L1 penalty. L2 shrinks coefficients and leaves them non-zero.

options.text: The model's bias decreases.
options.why: Bias increases as the model is constrained.

questions.explain: Regularization trades variance for bias. In scikit-learn, alpha is the strength for Ridge and Lasso, and C is its inverse for logistic regression and SVMs.

questions.title: Nearest neighbors in practice
questions.stem: Select the true statements about k-nearest neighbors.

options.text: The cost of a prediction grows with the size of the training set.
options.why: Each prediction searches the stored training points.

options.text: Features with larger scales dominate the distance unless you scale them.
options.why: Standardize before computing distances.

options.text: Performance tends to drop as you add irrelevant features.
options.why: Noise dimensions drown out the useful distances.

options.text: Training is slow because the model fits many parameters.
options.why: Training only stores the data. The work happens at prediction time.

options.text: A larger k makes the decision boundary more jagged.
options.why: A larger k averages over more neighbors and smooths the boundary.

questions.explain: k-NN is simple and has no training step, but it needs scaled, relevant features and gets slow and unreliable in high dimensions.

questions.title: Rare disease screening
questions.stem:
A screening model looks for a disease that affects 0.5% of patients. Missing a case is very costly, and a false alarm leads to a cheap follow-up test.

Which metric should guide your choice of threshold?

options.text: Recall
options.why: It measures the share of actual cases you catch, which is what the costs care about.

options.text: Accuracy
options.why: Predicting "healthy" for everyone scores 99.5%.

options.text: Precision
options.why: False alarms are cheap here, so precision is the secondary concern.

options.text: Specificity
options.why: It measures how well you clear healthy patients, not how many cases you catch.

options.text: R squared
options.why: That is a regression metric.

questions.explain: When misses cost far more than false alarms, lower the threshold to raise recall, and accept more false positives as long as the follow-up stays affordable.

questions.title: Tuning and validation
questions.stem: Select the true statements about hyperparameter tuning.

options.text: By default, GridSearchCV refits the best configuration on the whole training set.
options.why: refit=True is the default, and best_estimator_ holds the refitted model.

options.text: Random search can cover a large space with fewer fits than a full grid.
options.why: It samples configurations instead of trying every combination.

options.text: Nested cross-validation separates tuning from performance estimation.
options.why: The inner loop tunes and the outer loop scores.

options.text: Picking the model with the best test-set score and reporting that score gives an unbiased estimate.
options.why: Selecting on the test set makes its score optimistic.

options.text: 10-fold cross-validation always gives a lower error estimate than 5-fold.
options.why: More folds change the bias and variance of the estimate. They don't guarantee a lower number.

questions.explain: Keep three roles apart: training data fits the model, validation folds choose the settings, and untouched test data reports the result once.

questions.title: PCA
questions.stem: Select the true statements about principal component analysis.

options.text: The principal components are uncorrelated with each other.
options.why: They are orthogonal directions of variance.

options.text: PCA should be fitted on the training data only.
options.why: Fitting on all rows leaks information from the test set.

options.text: PCA uses the target to find its directions.
options.why: It is unsupervised and looks only at the features.

options.text: Features should usually be standardized before PCA.
options.why: Otherwise the features with the largest scales dominate the components.

options.text: The first component explains the least variance.
options.why: Components are ordered from most to least variance.

questions.explain: PCA rotates the features onto directions of decreasing variance. Because it ignores the target, a low-variance direction it discards can still be predictive.

questions.title: Reading coefficients
questions.stem:
A logistic regression for churn has a coefficient of 0.7 on the number of support tickets and -0.03 on tenure in months.

Select the correct readings.

options.text: Each extra ticket multiplies the odds of churn by about 2, holding tenure fixed.
options.why: e to the power 0.7 is 2.01.

options.text: Each extra ticket raises the probability of churn by 0.7.
options.why: Coefficients act on the log-odds, not on the probability.

options.text: Longer tenure is associated with lower odds of churn.
options.why: The coefficient is negative.

options.text: The decision boundary is linear in the features.
options.why: The log-odds are a linear function of the features.

options.text: Tickets matter more than tenure because 0.7 is larger than 0.03.
options.why: The features have different units. Compare coefficients only after standardizing.

questions.explain: Exponentiate a coefficient to get an odds ratio. To compare the size of effects, put the features on the same scale first.

exercises.title: Collect the house data
exercises.desc:
An agency lists houses for sale and logs every online viewing. You have the raw files, with data up to 15 April 2023. Build one table with a row for each house.

Files

  • houses.csv: house_id, bedrooms, bathrooms, sqft_living, sqft_lot, floors, waterfront, condition_id, age.
  • house_conditions.csv: condition_id, condition.
  • house_views.csv: view_id, house_id, view_date, viewer_id.
  • house_viewers.csv: viewer_id, first_name, last_name, email, registration_date.
  • house_prices.csv: house_id, price.

Your task

Save collected.csv in the task folder. It has one row per house in houses.csv and these columns, in this order:

ColumnTypeMeaning
house_idintHouse identifier
bedroomsintNumber of bedrooms
bathroomsintNumber of bathrooms
sqft_livingintLiving area
sqft_lotintLot area
floorsfloatNumber of floors, for example 1.5
waterfrontint1 if the house faces the waterfront, otherwise 0
ageintAge of the house in years
num_viewsintViews of the house in the last 30 days of the data: 16 March 2023 to 15 April 2023, both days included
condition_namestrName of the condition, not its ID
priceintPrice of the house

You can use pandas, NumPy, and scikit-learn.
exercises.solution:
import pandas as pd

houses = pd.read_csv('houses.csv')
conds = pd.read_csv('house_conditions.csv')
prices = pd.read_csv('house_prices.csv')
views = pd.read_csv('house_views.csv', parse_dates=['view_date'])

# 1 Filter: 16 Mar to 15 Apr 2023, both days included
d = views['view_date']
recent = views[(d >= '2023-03-16') & (d < '2023-04-16')]

# 2 Aggregate to one row per key
n_views = recent.groupby('house_id').size().reset_index(name='num_views')

# 3 Left-join everything onto the base table
out = (houses
       .merge(n_views, on='house_id', how='left')
       .merge(conds, on='condition_id', how='left')
       .merge(prices, on='house_id', how='left'))
assert len(out) == len(houses)   # no rows lost or doubled

# 4 Fix nulls, names, types, and column order
out['num_views'] = out['num_views'].fillna(0).astype(int)
out = out.rename(columns={'condition': 'condition_name'})
cols = ['house_id', 'bedrooms', 'bathrooms', 'sqft_living', 'sqft_lot', 'floors',
        'waterfront', 'age', 'num_views', 'condition_name', 'price']
out[cols].to_csv('collected.csv', index=False)
hints: Work in four steps: filter the views, aggregate to one row per house, left-join onto houses, then fix nulls, names, types, and column order.
The window is 16 March to 15 April 2023 with both days included, and view_date carries a time of day. A safe filter is >= '2023-03-16' and < '2023-04-16'.
Houses with no views in the window have no match after the left join. Fill num_views with 0, then cast it to int.

exercises.title: Process without leakage
exercises.desc:
This dataset has the format of the table you built in the collection task. The values are different, so you can't reuse your earlier answer.

The data is split into a train set with 70% of the rows and a test set with the other 30%.

Files

  • data/train.csv: house_id, bedrooms, bathrooms, sqft_living, sqft_lot, floors, waterfront, age, num_views, condition_name, price.
  • data/test.csv: the same columns.

Your task

Apply these steps with pandas, NumPy, or scikit-learn:

  1. Fill the missing values in age with the mean age.
  2. Convert condition_name to numbers with ordinal encoding. Use scikit-learn's default order, which is alphabetical.
  3. Normalize sqft_living and sqft_lot with standard scaling.

Don't let information from the test set leak into the train set. Keep every row, the row order, and the column order.

Save the results in the task folder as processed_train.csv and processed_test.csv.
exercises.solution:
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.preprocessing import OrdinalEncoder, StandardScaler

train = pd.read_csv('data/train.csv')
test = pd.read_csv('data/test.csv')

# 1 Impute: the statistic comes from train only
age_mean = train['age'].mean()
train['age'] = train['age'].fillna(age_mean)
test['age'] = test['age'].fillna(age_mean)

# 2 Ordinal encode: fit on train, transform both
cat = ['condition_name']
enc = OrdinalEncoder()      # alphabetical unless you say otherwise
train[cat] = enc.fit_transform(train[cat])
test[cat] = enc.transform(test[cat])

# 3 Standard scale: fit on train, transform both
num = ['sqft_living', 'sqft_lot']
sc = StandardScaler()
train[num] = sc.fit_transform(train[num])
test[num] = sc.transform(test[num])

# 4 Save both files
train.to_csv('processed_train.csv', index=False)
test.to_csv('processed_test.csv', index=False)
hints: Every statistic comes from train: the mean age, the category order, and the scaling mean and standard deviation.
For each step, fit on train, then transform train and test. The test set only ever gets transform.
StandardScaler divides by the population standard deviation (ddof=0). pandas .std() uses ddof=1 unless you pass ddof=0.

exercises.title: Predict house prices
exercises.desc:
This dataset has the format of the files you saved in the processing task. The values are different.

The data is split three ways: a train set with 70% of the rows, a validation set with 15%, and a test set with 15%. The test set has no prices. It is used to score your model on unseen data.

Files

  • train.csv: house_id, bedrooms, bathrooms, sqft_living, sqft_lot, floors, waterfront, age, num_views, condition_name, price.
  • val.csv: the same columns.
  • test.csv: the same columns without price.

Your task

Predict price for every house in test.csv. This is a free-form task: use any model and any of pandas, NumPy, and scikit-learn.

The metric is mean absolute error (MAE). The bar is an MAE below 27,000 on the test set.

Save your predictions in the task folder as predictions.csv, one row per test row in the same order, with this format:

price
123456.789
234567.89
345678.9
exercises.solution:
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor, HistGradientBoostingRegressor
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error

# 1 Load, name the target, list the features
train = pd.read_csv('train.csv')
val = pd.read_csv('val.csv')
test = pd.read_csv('test.csv')
target = 'price'
feats = list(test.columns.drop('house_id'))

# 2 Compare three model families on validation
models = {
    'ridge': Ridge(),
    'rf': RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=300, random_state=42, n_jobs=-1),
    'hgb': HistGradientBoostingRegressor(loss='absolute_error', random_state=42)}
scores = {}
for name, m in models.items():
    m.fit(train[feats], train[target])
    scores[name] = mean_absolute_error(val[target], m.predict(val[feats]))
    print(name, round(scores[name]))

# 3 Refit the winner on train + val, then predict test
best = models[min(scores, key=scores.get)]
full = pd.concat([train, val], ignore_index=True)
best.fit(full[feats], full[target])
out = pd.DataFrame({'price': best.predict(test[feats])})
out.to_csv('predictions.csv', index=False)
hints: Save a valid predictions.csv from any quick model first. Improve it after that.
Compare a linear model, a random forest, and gradient boosting on val.csv with mean_absolute_error.
The metric is MAE, so try HistGradientBoostingRegressor(loss='absolute_error'). Refit the winner on train plus val before you predict test.

exercises.title: Top 3 products per category
exercises.desc:
The shop wants its best sellers. Find the three products with the highest revenue in each category.

Files

  • orders.csv: order_id, customer_id, order_date, status. The status is completed, cancelled, or returned.
  • order_items.csv: order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price.
  • products.csv: product_id, product_name, category.

import pandas as pd

orders = pd.read_csv('orders.csv')
items = pd.read_csv('order_items.csv')

items['amount'] = items['quantity'] * items['unit_price']
totals = items.groupby('order_id')['amount'].sum().round(2).rename('order_total').reset_index()

h['ts'] = pd.to_datetime(h['order_date'])
h = h.sort_values(['customer_id', 'ts', 'order_id'])

import json
import pandas as pd

# Nested JSON: one row per store, with the region carried down
with open('stores.json') as f:
    regions = json.load(f)
stores = pd.json_normalize(regions, record_path='stores', meta=['region'])

              .merge(stores, on='store_id', how='left'))

exercises.title: Impute, flag, and one-hot encode
exercises.desc:
A dealer's listings have gaps in mileage_km and fuel, and two text columns that a model can't read. The data is split into a train set (70%) and a test set (30%).

Files

  • data/train.csv: car_id, brand, body, fuel, year, mileage_km, engine_cc, power_hp, condition, price.
  • data/test.csv: the same columns.

Your task

  1. Add mileage_missing: 1 where mileage_km is missing, otherwise 0.
  2. Fill the missing mileage_km values with the median mileage of the train set.
  3. Fill the missing fuel values with the most frequent fuel in the train set.
  4. One-hot encode fuel and body. Learn the levels from the train set. Name the new columns fuel_<level> and body_<level>, with levels in alphabetical order, holding the integers 0 and 1. A level that the train set never saw gets 0 in every column of that feature. Drop the original fuel and body columns.

The saved files have these columns, in this order: car_id, brand, year, mileage_km, engine_cc, power_hp, condition, price, mileage_missing, fuel_diesel, fuel_electric, fuel_hybrid, fuel_petrol, body_hatch, body_sedan, body_suv, body_wagon.

Don't let information from the test set leak into the train set. Keep every row and the row order. Save the results in the task folder as processed_train.csv and processed_test.csv.

import pandas as pd
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder

train = pd.read_csv('data/train.csv')
test = pd.read_csv('data/test.csv')

# 1 Flag first, then fill. Both statistics come from train
med = train['mileage_km'].median()
top_fuel = train['fuel'].mode()[0]
for df in (train, test):
    df['mileage_missing'] = df['mileage_km'].isna().astype(int)
    df['mileage_km'] = df['mileage_km'].fillna(med)
    df['fuel'] = df['fuel'].fillna(top_fuel)

# 2 One-hot: fit on train, transform both. Unseen levels become all zeros
cat = ['fuel', 'body']
oh = OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown='ignore', sparse_output=False)
oh.fit(train[cat])
names = oh.get_feature_names_out(cat)

def encode(df):
    hot = pd.DataFrame(oh.transform(df[cat]).astype(int), columns=names, index=df.index)
    return df.drop(columns=cat).join(hot)

encode(train).to_csv('processed_train.csv', index=False)
encode(test).to_csv('processed_test.csv', index=False)

The same kind of listings, this time with no missing values. A few engine sizes are far outside the usual range.

  3. Add power_band: the quartile of power_hp, as an integer from 0 (lowest) to 3. Use pd.qcut with 4 bins on the train set, and reuse its bin edges for the test set. Test values below the lowest train edge go to band 0, and values above the highest go to band 3.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

train = pd.read_csv('data/train.csv')
test = pd.read_csv('data/test.csv')

# IQR fences from train
q1, q3 = train['engine_cc'].quantile([0.25, 0.75])
iqr = q3 - q1
lo, hi = q1 - 1.5 * iqr, q3 + 1.5 * iqr

# Quartile edges from train, opened at both ends to catch unseen extremes
_, edges = pd.qcut(train['power_hp'], 4, retbins=True)
edges[0], edges[-1] = -np.inf, np.inf

for df in (train, test):
    df['engine_cc'] = df['engine_cc'].clip(lo, hi)
    df['mileage_log'] = np.log1p(df['mileage_km'])
    df['power_band'] = pd.cut(df['power_hp'], bins=edges, labels=False)

train.to_csv('processed_train.csv', index=False)
test.to_csv('processed_test.csv', index=False)

exercises.title: Ordinal order, min-max, and z-scores
exercises.desc:
The same kind of listings, with no missing values. Prepare three columns for a distance-based model.

Files

  • data/train.csv: car_id, brand, body, fuel, year, mileage_km, engine_cc, power_hp, condition, price.
  • data/test.csv: the same columns.

Your task

  1. Encode condition as an integer by quality: poor 0, fair 1, good 2, excellent 3.
  2. Min-max scale year and power_hp with the train set: subtract the train minimum, then divide by the train maximum minus the train minimum. Don't clip the test set, so test values can fall below 0 or above 1.
  3. Add engine_z: the z-score of engine_cc, using the train mean and the train population standard deviation (ddof=0).
  4. Add is_outlier: 1 where the absolute value of engine_z is above 3, otherwise 0.

import pandas as pd
from sklearn.preprocessing import MinMaxScaler, OrdinalEncoder, StandardScaler

train = pd.read_csv('data/train.csv')
test = pd.read_csv('data/test.csv')

# Each transformer is fitted on train only
enc = OrdinalEncoder(categories=[['poor', 'fair', 'good', 'excellent']]).fit(train[['condition']])
num = ['year', 'power_hp']
mm = MinMaxScaler().fit(train[num])
z = StandardScaler().fit(train[['engine_cc']])        # population standard deviation

for df in (train, test):
    df['condition'] = enc.transform(df[['condition']])[:, 0].astype(int)
    df[num] = mm.transform(df[num])
    df['engine_z'] = z.transform(df[['engine_cc']])[:, 0]
    df['is_outlier'] = (df['engine_z'].abs() > 3).astype(int)

train.to_csv('processed_train.csv', index=False)
test.to_csv('processed_test.csv', index=False)

exercises.title: Clear a precision bar
exercises.desc:
A card issuer wants to block suspicious transactions automatically. A blocked genuine payment annoys a customer, so the model must be right when it raises a flag.

The data is split three ways: train, validation, and test. The test set has no labels. About 8% of transactions are fraud, and some genuine payments look a lot like it.

Files

  • train.csv: tx_id, amount, hour, merchant_category, country_match, n_tx_24h, account_age_days, device_score, is_fraud. merchant_category is text, and device_score has missing values.
  • val.csv: the same columns.
  • test.csv: the same columns without is_fraud.

Your task

Predict is_fraud for every row of test.csv. Use any model.

The bars, measured on the hidden test labels: precision of at least 0.90 and recall of at least 0.35.

Save predictions.csv in the task folder with one column named is_fraud that holds 0 or 1, one row per test row, in the same order.
exercises.solution:
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import precision_score, recall_score

train = pd.read_csv('train.csv')
val = pd.read_csv('val.csv')
test = pd.read_csv('test.csv')
target = 'is_fraud'

# 1 Features: one-hot the text column, align every set to train's columns
def features(df, cols=None):
    X = pd.get_dummies(df.drop(columns=['tx_id', target], errors='ignore'),
                       columns=['merchant_category'], dtype=int)
    return X if cols is None else X.reindex(columns=cols, fill_value=0)

X = features(train)
med = X['device_score'].median()                 # learned on train
X = X.fillna({'device_score': med})
X_val = features(val, X.columns).fillna({'device_score': med})
X_test = features(test, X.columns).fillna({'device_score': med})

# 2 Fit, then score probabilities on validation
clf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, random_state=42, n_jobs=-1)
clf.fit(X, train[target])
p_val = clf.predict_proba(X_val)[:, 1]

# 3 Lowest threshold whose validation precision clears the bar with a margin
for t in [0.50, 0.55, 0.60, 0.65, 0.70, 0.75, 0.80, 0.85, 0.90]:
    lab = (p_val >= t).astype(int)
    p = precision_score(val[target], lab, zero_division=0)
    r = recall_score(val[target], lab)
    print(t, round(p, 3), round(r, 3))
    if p >= 0.95:
        break

# 4 Apply that threshold to test and save labels
pred = (clf.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1] >= t).astype(int)
pd.DataFrame({target: pred}).to_csv('predictions.csv', index=False)

Scan thresholds from 0.5 to 0.9 on val.csv. Keep the lowest one whose precision clears the bar with a few points of margin, then apply it to test.

exercises.desc:
Before you tune anything, you want an honest comparison of a linear model and a few random forests. Report 5-fold cross-validation scores for four candidates.

Your task

The target is churned. The features are every column except customer_id and churned. Score each model with ROC AUC, using this splitter for all of them:

StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)

The four models, in this order:

  • logreg: make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))
  • forest_2, forest_4, forest_8: RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=50, max_depth=d, random_state=42) with d equal to 2, 4, and 8

Save cv_report.csv with one row per model, in the order above:

import pandas as pd
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold, cross_val_score
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

train = pd.read_csv('train.csv')
X = train.drop(columns=['customer_id', 'churned'])
y = train['churned']

cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
models = {'logreg': make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))}
for depth in [2, 4, 8]:
    models[f'forest_{depth}'] = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=50, max_depth=depth, random_state=42)

rows = []
for name, model in models.items():
    s = cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=cv, scoring='roc_auc')
    rows.append({'model': name, 'mean_auc': s.mean(), 'std_auc': s.std()})   # NumPy std: ddof=0

report = pd.DataFrame(rows)
best = report.loc[report['mean_auc'].idxmax(), 'model']
report.round({'mean_auc': 4, 'std_auc': 4}).to_csv('cv_report.csv', index=False)
with open('best_model.txt', 'w') as f:
    f.write(best)

exercises.desc:
This dataset has the format of the table you built in the collection task. The values are different, so you can't reuse your earlier answer. It is split into a train set (70%) and a test set (30%).

Files

  2. Fill the missing values in region with the most frequent region in the train set.
  3. One-hot encode region and plan_name. Learn the levels from the train set. Name the new columns region_<level> and plan_name_<level>, with levels in alphabetical order, holding the integers 0 and 1. A level that the train set never saw gets 0 in every column of that feature. Drop the original two columns.
  4. Min-max scale tenure_days and monthly_fee with the train set: subtract the train minimum, then divide by the train maximum minus the train minimum.

The saved files have these columns, in this order: customer_id, monthly_fee, tenure_days, avg_data_gb, tickets_90d, unresolved_tickets, churned, region_East, region_North, region_South, region_West, plan_name_Basic, plan_name_Family, plan_name_Max, plan_name_Plus.

import pandas as pd
from sklearn.preprocessing import MinMaxScaler, OneHotEncoder

train = pd.read_csv('data/train.csv')
test = pd.read_csv('data/test.csv')

# 1 and 2: impute with train statistics
med = train['avg_data_gb'].median()
top_region = train['region'].mode()[0]
for df in (train, test):
    df['avg_data_gb'] = df['avg_data_gb'].fillna(med)
    df['region'] = df['region'].fillna(top_region)

# 4: min-max scale, fitted on train
num = ['tenure_days', 'monthly_fee']
mm = MinMaxScaler().fit(train[num])
train[num] = mm.transform(train[num])
test[num] = mm.transform(test[num])

# 3: one-hot, fitted on train. Unseen levels become all zeros
cat = ['region', 'plan_name']
oh = OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown='ignore', sparse_output=False).fit(train[cat])
names = oh.get_feature_names_out(cat)

def encode(df):
    hot = pd.DataFrame(oh.transform(df[cat]).astype(int), columns=names, index=df.index)
    return df.drop(columns=cat).join(hot)

encode(train).to_csv('processed_train.csv', index=False)
encode(test).to_csv('processed_test.csv', index=False)

exercises.title: Predict churn
exercises.desc:
This dataset has the format of the files you saved in the processing task. The values are different.

It is split three ways: train (60%), validation (16%), and test (24%). The test set has no churned column. About one customer in five churns.

Files

  • train.csv: customer_id, monthly_fee, tenure_days, avg_data_gb, tickets_90d, unresolved_tickets, churned, region_East, region_North, region_South, region_West, plan_name_Basic, plan_name_Family, plan_name_Max, plan_name_Plus.
  • val.csv: the same columns.
  • test.csv: the same columns without churned.

Your task

Predict churned for every customer in test.csv. This is a free-form task: use any model.

The metric is the F1 score of the churn class. The bar is an F1 of at least 0.60 on the test set.

Save predictions.csv in the task folder with one column named churned that holds 0 or 1, one row per test row, in the same order.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingClassifier, RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import f1_score

train = pd.read_csv('train.csv')
val = pd.read_csv('val.csv')
test = pd.read_csv('test.csv')
target = 'churned'
feats = list(test.columns.drop('customer_id'))

# 1 Compare model families, each at its best F1 threshold on validation
models = {
    'logreg': LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000),
    'rf': RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, min_samples_leaf=5, random_state=42, n_jobs=-1),
    'hgb': HistGradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=42)}
grid = np.arange(0.20, 0.61, 0.05)
best = (None, 0.5, -1.0)
for name, m in models.items():
    m.fit(train[feats], train[target])
    p = m.predict_proba(val[feats])[:, 1]
    f1s = [f1_score(val[target], p >= t) for t in grid]
    i = int(np.argmax(f1s))
    print(name, round(float(grid[i]), 2), round(f1s[i], 3))
    if f1s[i] > best[2]:
        best = (name, float(grid[i]), f1s[i])

# 2 Refit the winner on train + val, predict test at the chosen threshold
name, t, _ = best
full = pd.concat([train, val], ignore_index=True)
model = models[name].fit(full[feats], full[target])
pred = (model.predict_proba(test[feats])[:, 1] >= t).astype(int)
pd.DataFrame({target: pred}).to_csv('predictions.csv', index=False)

A lender wants to predict which loans default. You have a snapshot of its records taken on 31 December 2024. Build one table with a row for each loan.

  • loans.csv: loan_id, applicant_id, branch_id, amount, term_months, interest_rate, start_date.
  • applicants.csv: applicant_id, age, income, employment_years, grade.
  • branches.csv: branch_id, branch_name, city. This file uses semicolons as separators.
  • payments.csv: the instalment schedule, with payment_id, loan_id, due_date, paid_date, amount_due, amount_paid. paid_date is empty while an instalment is unpaid. The schedule includes instalments that fall due after the snapshot.

Your task

Save collected.csv in the task folder. It has one row per loan in loans.csv, sorted by loan_id, with these columns in this order:

ColumnTypeMeaning
loan_idintLoan identifier
amountintLoan amount
term_monthsintLoan term
interest_ratefloatInterest rate
ageintApplicant's age
incomeintApplicant's income
employment_yearsintApplicant's years in employment
gradestrApplicant's credit grade
branch_citystrCity of the loan's branch
n_dueintInstalments with a due_date on or before 31 December 2024
n_lateintOf those, the instalments that were paid after their due date or are still unpaid
late_ratiofloatn_late divided by n_due, rounded to 3 decimals. 0 when no instalment is due yet

import pandas as pd

loans = pd.read_csv('loans.csv')
applicants = pd.read_csv('applicants.csv')
branches = pd.read_csv('branches.csv', sep=';')
pay = pd.read_csv('payments.csv', parse_dates=['due_date', 'paid_date'])

# Instalments that are due by the snapshot. Unpaid ones have no paid_date and count as late
due = pay[pay['due_date'] <= '2024-12-31'].copy()
due['late'] = due['paid_date'].isna() | (due['paid_date'] > due['due_date'])
counts = due.groupby('loan_id').agg(n_due=('payment_id', 'count'), n_late=('late', 'sum')).reset_index()
paid = pay.groupby('loan_id')['amount_paid'].sum().round(2).rename('total_paid').reset_index()
city = branches[['branch_id', 'city']].rename(columns={'city': 'branch_city'})

out = (loans
       .merge(applicants, on='applicant_id', how='left')
       .merge(city, on='branch_id', how='left')
       .merge(counts, on='loan_id', how='left')
       .merge(paid, on='loan_id', how='left'))
assert len(out) == len(loans)

for col in ['n_due', 'n_late']:
    out[col] = out[col].fillna(0).astype(int)
out['total_paid'] = out['total_paid'].fillna(0)
out['late_ratio'] = (out['n_late'] / out['n_due']).fillna(0).round(3)     # 0 / 0 gives NaN

cols = ['loan_id', 'amount', 'term_months', 'interest_rate', 'age', 'income', 'employment_years', 'grade',
        'branch_city', 'n_due', 'n_late', 'late_ratio', 'total_paid']
out.sort_values('loan_id')[cols].to_csv('collected.csv', index=False)

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

train = pd.read_csv('data/train.csv')
test = pd.read_csv('data/test.csv')

# 1 Group-wise median, learned on train
med = train.groupby('grade')['income'].median()
for df in (train, test):

# 2 IQR fences on the filled train income

    df['income_log'] = np.log1p(df['income'])                              # 3
    df['grade'] = df['grade'].map({'A': 0, 'B': 1, 'C': 2, 'D': 3})        # 4

exercises.desc:
This dataset has the format of the files you saved in the processing task. The values are different. branch_city is still text.

It is split three ways: train, validation, and test. The test set has no defaulted column. About one loan in six defaults.

Files

  • train.csv: loan_id, amount, term_months, interest_rate, age, income, employment_years, grade, branch_city, n_due, n_late, late_ratio, total_paid, defaulted, income_log.
  • val.csv: the same columns.
  • test.csv: the same columns without defaulted.

Your task

Estimate the probability of default for every loan in test.csv. This is a free-form task: use any model.

The metric is ROC AUC. The bar is an AUC of at least 0.80 on the test set.

Save predictions.csv in the task folder with one column named default_probability that holds a number from 0 to 1, one row per test row, in the same order.

import pandas as pd
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingClassifier, RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

train = pd.read_csv('train.csv')
val = pd.read_csv('val.csv')
test = pd.read_csv('test.csv')
target = 'defaulted'

# 1 Features: one-hot the text column, align every set to train's columns
def features(df, cols=None):
    X = pd.get_dummies(df.drop(columns=['loan_id', target], errors='ignore'), columns=['branch_city'], dtype=int)
    return X if cols is None else X.reindex(columns=cols, fill_value=0)

X = features(train)
X_val, X_test = features(val, X.columns), features(test, X.columns)

# 2 Compare model families by validation AUC, on probabilities
models = {
    'logreg': make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)),
    'rf': RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, min_samples_leaf=5, random_state=42, n_jobs=-1),
    'hgb': HistGradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=42)}
scores = {}
for name, m in models.items():
    m.fit(X, train[target])
    scores[name] = roc_auc_score(val[target], m.predict_proba(X_val)[:, 1])
    print(name, round(scores[name], 3))

# 3 Refit the winner on train + val, save probabilities for test
best = models[max(scores, key=scores.get)]
best.fit(pd.concat([X, X_val]), pd.concat([train[target], val[target]]))
out = pd.DataFrame({'default_probability': best.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]})
out.to_csv('predictions.csv', index=False)

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

BAR = 0.8
METRIC = f'ROC AUC on the hidden test labels is at least {BAR:.2f}'


def auc(y, score):
    rank = pd.Series(score).rank(method='average').to_numpy()
    pos = y == 1
    n1, n0 = int(pos.sum()), int((~pos).sum())
    return float((rank[pos].sum() - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) / (n1 * n0))


def grade(c):
    c.plan('predictions.csv is saved in the task folder',
           'predictions.csv has no index column',
           'One column, named default_probability',
           'One prediction per test row',
           'Every prediction is a number from 0 to 1',
           (METRIC, True))
    got = c.output('predictions.csv')
    if got is None:
        return
    if not c.check('One column, named default_probability', list(got.columns) == ['default_probability'],
                   'Found these columns: ' + ', '.join(map(str, got.columns)) + '.',
                   'Save a DataFrame that holds only the default_probability column.'):
        return
    truth = c.secret('truth.csv')
    if not c.check('One prediction per test row', len(got) == len(truth),
                   f'test.csv has {len(truth):,} rows and predictions.csv has {len(got):,}.',
                   'Predict on test.csv and keep its row order.'):
        return
    p = pd.to_numeric(got['default_probability'], errors='coerce')
    if not c.check('Every prediction is a number from 0 to 1', bool(p.notna().all() and p.between(0, 1).all()),
                   'Some values are missing or fall outside 0 to 1.', 'Save predict_proba(X)[:, 1].'):
        return
    score = auc(truth['defaulted'].to_numpy(), p.to_numpy())
    labels = p.nunique() <= 2
    c.note(f'ROC AUC {score:.3f} (bar {BAR:.2f}).')
    c.check(METRIC, score >= BAR, f'Your AUC is {score:.3f}.',
            'These look like 0 and 1 labels. AUC scores a ranking, so save predict_proba(X)[:, 1], not predict(X).' if labels
            else 'Compare a scaled logistic regression with tree ensembles on val.csv, and use every informative column.')
